catalog_quote: Wat het leggen van de klemtoon betreft merkt VAN EECHOUD op, dat door hem nog geen regels konden worden vastgesteld. Ik meen te dien aanzien het volgende te hebben bemerkt. Bij tweelettergrepige woorden valt de klemtoon in het Dèms, maar vooral in het Monisch als regel op de voorlaatste lettergreep, bijv. M. àgi = stengel, [...] D. àmbò = schoonmoeder, bijěm = bataten, bela = vogel, kàbo = mes, kalò = groot, majoe = zout, wobit = slang. Voorbeelden van het omgekeerde zijn: M. amè = traan, èmbai = lui; D. ali = haar, àmbi = penis, màboei = kalebas, mědjà = rijp, měning = juist, nèndèm = zoet, nasim = honger, pani = maagd, oràk = bepijlen, tànè = mannenhuis. In enkele gevallen viel te constateren, dat een verplaatsing van de klemtoon aan het woord een andere betekenis gaf, bijv. M. àmoe = neus en àmoe = luis, oewai = danshuis en oewai = lever; D. àmà = één en àmà = moeder. Bij drielettergrepige woorden kon ik geen vaste regel ontdekken, alhoewel in het Monisch het accent meestal op de derde van achteren, maar ook wel op de eindlettergreep valt; in de Dèm-taal echter nu eens op de derde van achteren, dan weer op de laatste lettergreep. [...] In samengestelde woorden rust het hoofdaccent vaak op de voorlaatste, doch evenzeer op alle andere lettergrepen. Hierin heb ik geen regels kunnen ontdekken.

new_statements.translation: In disyllabic words the stress in Dem — but above all in Moni — falls as a rule on the penultimate syllable, e.g. [...] D. àmbò 'mother-in-law', bijèm 'sweet potato', bela 'bird', kàbo 'knife', kalò 'big', majoe 'salt', wobit 'snake'. Examples of the reverse are: [...] D. ali 'hair', àmbi 'penis', màboei 'calabash', [...] In a few cases it could be observed that a shift of the stress gave the word a different meaning, e.g. [...] D. àmà 'one' and àmà 'mother'. In trisyllabic words I could discover no fixed rule, [...] in the Dem language, however, [it falls] now on the third from the end, now on the last syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No fixed stress position: disyllables tend to penultimate (initial) stress but a good number are final-stressed and at least one pair is distinguished by stress alone ('one' vs 'mother'); trisyllables vary between antepenultimate and final stress with no rule the author could find; in compounds the main accent is often penultimate but may sit on any syllable. Stress is therefore recorded per word (roman = stressed syllable) in Le Roux's 673-item Dem list, pp. 852-862.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described; for compounds only a 'hoofdaccent' (main accent) is mentioned, 'often on the penult, but equally on all other syllables' (p. 793-794).
new_statements.exceptions: Final-stressed disyllables listed (ali, àmbi, màboei, mědjà, měning, nèndèm, nasim, pani, oràk, tànè); meaning-distinguishing stress (àmà 'one' vs àmà 'mother'); p. 794: stress shifts with sentence rhythm ('zinsmaat') and especially in contractions/compounds (èp arò > èwarò, koenoe sisi > koenoesì, ènggio ali > ènggèli); speakers of different tribes stress the same names differently.
new_statements.domain_note: Impressionistic word-level observations by an explorer-ethnographer (KNAG expedition 1939, c. 3 months at Tombe on the upper Rouffaer with chief Igoen as main consultant, checked against other Dem speakers); citation forms elicited in isolation; the author explicitly treats Dem and Moni together and says the penult tendency is stronger in Moni than in Dem.
new_statements.identity_note: Le Roux's 'Dèm(-taal)' is Dem [dem], demm1245: data (673 words, sentences) collected in 1926 and mainly 1939 at Tombe in the Nògòlò valley on the upper Rouffaer River, north of the Western Dani, from chief Igoen and other Dem speakers. The stress remarks are made jointly for Dem and Moni (Le Roux contrasts them), so only the clauses marked 'D.'/'in het Dèms'/'in de Dèm-taal' apply to demm1245. No modern grammar, sketch or phonology of Dem exists (Glottolog desc refs = 0; Hammarström 2010 calls Le Roux 1950 the main source).

sources.note: pp. 792-793: in disyllables stress falls as a rule on the penult in Dem (more consistently in Moni), with listed Dem counter-examples stressed on the final; a stress shift can change meaning (D. àmà 'one' vs àmà 'mother'); for trisyllables no fixed rule — in Dem now antepenult, now final; compounds: main accent often penult but equally any syllable, no rule found; p. 794 stress shifts with sentence rhythm and in contractions. Vowels/consonants of Dem described pp. 787-791. The 673-word Dem list (pp. 852-862) marks stress typographically (stressed syllable roman, unstressed italic; cf. fn. p.…
